content: A systematic review was conducted to evaluate the care of children infected with HIV who also suffer from severe acute malnutrition (SAM). This work, commissioned by the World Health Organization (WHO), was authored by Mark Manary, Indi Trehan, and Juana Willumsen. The authors declared no conflicts of interest. Background Significant progress has been made in managing childhood SAM with the introduction of ready-to-use therapeutic foods (RUTFs). However, the high burden of HIV/AIDS continues to impede efforts to reduce mortality and morbidity, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. While therapeutic protocols for SAM in both inpatient and outpatient settings have reduced mortality and morbidity, children with both SAM and HIV still experience poor outcomes. A meta-analysis revealed that HIV-infected children with SAM are nearly three times more likely to die during nutritional rehabilitation compared to their HIV-negative counterparts. This highlights the need to assess whether HIV-infected children with SAM require different clinical care and nutritional interventions due to their unique pathophysiology. HIV-infected children with SAM face a worse prognosis than uninfected children. Several physiological and social factors contribute to the higher failure rates of nutritional therapy in this population. These include altered glucose and lipid metabolism (due to HIV or antiretroviral therapy [ART]), micronutrient deficiencies, altered pharmacokinetics of antibiotics and antiretroviral medications, gastrointestinal side effects of antiretrovirals, higher rates of diarrhea and malabsorption, mitochondrial dysfunction, reduced antioxidant capacity, frequent coinfections, and food insecurity. Severe wasting in HIV-infected children is classified as a WHO Stage IV condition, qualifying them for lifelong ART. However, the optimal timing and dosing of ART in children with SAM remain unclear due to their unstable and changing physiology. Methodology A systematic review of studies published between 1985 and 2011 was conducted. Observational and randomized studies in English, French, or Spanish were included. The review sought to address specific clinical questions regarding the timing and dosing of ART, the value of vitamin A supplementation, strategies for managing diarrhea, and optimal feeding regimens for HIV-infected children with SAM. The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach. Key Findings 1. Timing and Dosing of ART in HIV-Infected Children with SAM The quality of evidence for this question was very low due to the lack of prospective randomized trials. Observational studies suggested that malnourished children with lower weight-for-age z-scores (< -3) had higher mortality rates when initiated on ART. However, no studies directly addressed the timing of ART initiation in relation to SAM treatment. Concerns about ART toxicity and its potential to exacerbate the already perturbed physiology of malnourished children have led to recommendations to delay ART initiation until nutritional stabilization. However, this approach remains controversial, and further research is needed. 2. Vitamin A Supplementation Vitamin A supplementation is recommended for children hospitalized with SAM and for all children aged 6 months to 5 years to support growth and reduce mortality. However, no studies directly addressed the safety or efficacy of vitamin A supplementation specifically in HIV-infected children with SAM. Current guidelines recommend administering vitamin A to HIV-infected children with SAM in the same manner as uninfected children. 3. Management of Diarrhea in HIV-Infected Children with SAM Acute diarrheal disease is a leading cause of death among children, and HIV-infected children with SAM are at particularly high risk. The quality of evidence for this question was very low. No studies directly addressed the most effective diagnostic or therapeutic strategies for managing diarrhea in this population. Zinc supplementation, which is recommended for children with SAM and diarrhea, is considered safe for HIV-infected children. Until further data are available, HIV-infected children with SAM and diarrhea should receive the same therapeutic feeds and zinc supplementation as uninfected children. 4. Optimal Feeding Regimens The quality of evidence for this question was also very low. Studies comparing recovery rates between HIV-infected and uninfected children with SAM found no significant differences in nutritional recovery among survivors, although mortality rates were higher in HIV-infected children. Trials of dietary supplements, such as probiotics or prebiotics, failed to demonstrate significant differences in recovery rates. Further research is needed to determine whether standard therapeutic feeding regimens are sufficient for HIV-infected children with SAM or if modifications are required. Conclusions There is a lack of high-quality evidence to guide the management of HIV-infected children with SAM. Clinicians must rely on general medical principles and evidence from other patient populations to inform their care. Early initiation of ART has been shown to reduce mortality and improve growth in HIV-infected children, but concerns about potential toxicity in malnourished children have led to delays in ART initiation. Further research is urgently needed to address the optimal timing and dosing of ART, the safety and efficacy of vitamin A supplementation, the management of diarrhea, and the adequacy of current feeding regimens for this vulnerable population.
